messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 35

**Karim**

Karim is a thirty-year-old tax inspector of Lebanese descent who sits across from his therapist with a careful stillness, the kind that looks composed until you notice his hands resting flat on his thighs, pressing down slightly, as though steadying himself against something invisible. He chooses his words the way he works through a financial audit — methodically, double-checking before committing — and yet even that precision occasionally fails him when the conversation turns to the evening fourteen months ago that split his life into a before and after.

It was a Tuesday in late autumn. Karim was driving home from a late site visit, a route he had taken hundreds of times, when a lorry ran a red light at speed and struck the driver's side of his car. The vehicle spun and rolled. He remembers the sound — a tearing, compressing roar — and then a strange, suspended silence before he understood he was upside down, glass in his hair, unable to move his left arm. He was conscious throughout. Paramedics took forty minutes to cut him free. He kept thinking, with odd bureaucratic clarity, that he hadn't filed a particular report before leaving the office.

He recovered physically within three months. A fractured clavicle, lacerations, bruised ribs. His marriage, already strained, did not survive the aftermath. His ex-wife, Nadia, found his withdrawal unbearable — the way he stopped sleeping in their bed because lying flat made him feel trapped, the way he flinched at ordinary sounds, the way he was simply no longer present even when he was standing in the same room. They divorced eight months ago. Karim speaks of this without apparent bitterness, as if it, too, was an outcome he had audited and accepted.

He drives now only when he has no alternative, and even then he takes routes that avoid the intersection where the collision happened, adding twenty minutes to his commute. On the motorway, his chest tightens and his vision narrows. Twice he has pulled over and sat on the hard shoulder, breathing, waiting for his heart rate to slow. He has not told his supervisor why he prefers to take the train to client visits.

At work, Karim functions. He is thorough and well-regarded, and the linear logic of tax codes offers him something reliable to hold onto. But concentration frays without warning. He will be cross-referencing figures and suddenly he is back inside the car, upside down, and the numbers on the screen mean nothing. He saves his work compulsively now, every few minutes, as though afraid something will be lost before he can secure it.

Sleep is the worst of it, he says quietly. He wakes between two and four in the morning with his pulse hammering, the dream always the same — not a replay, exactly, but a version in which no one comes. The paramedics never arrive. He is still there. He lies awake afterwards in his flat, listening to the street outside, and feels a loneliness he describes as physical, like a pressure behind the sternum.

He has stopped calling his parents as often. His mother asks why he sounds tired and he tells her he has been busy with year-end assessments. He does not want her to worry. He does not want, he admits, for anyone to see how much effort ordinary life currently requires.

What strikes his therapist most is the gap between how Karim presents — measured, self-sufficient, almost formal — and what he occasionally lets slip: that he sometimes sits in his parked car outside his building for ten or fifteen minutes before he can make himself go inside, that he has not listened to the radio since the accident because music makes him feel unexpectedly close to crying, that he misses, more than anything, the feeling of moving through the world without bracing for it.

He is here, he says, because he is tired of managing. He would like, at some point, to simply live.
